story.title: Ebola Outbreak in DR Congo Becomes Deadliest in History
story.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has officially become the deadliest in the country's history, with at least 2,325 reported deaths. This surpasses the toll from the previous outbreak between 2018 and 2020. Current data indicates that confirmed cases have risen to 4,945, with one death occurring approximately every 30 minutes.

The outbreak reportedly began months before it was officially declared in May, complicating response efforts due to factors such as rebel conflict and infrastructure challenges.

event_overview.title: About Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.subject: Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.summary: This is the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with epidemiologically linked cases reported in neighboring Uganda. The outbreak was declared in May 2026 and has expanded from its initial focus in northeastern DRC amid insecurity, population movement, and constraints on surveillance, isolation, and care.

facts.label: Start and official declaration
facts.value: DRC health authorities declared the country’s 17th recorded Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026, after the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease in samples associated with illness clusters in Ituri Province.

facts.label: Virus involved
facts.value: The event involves Bundibugyo virus disease, rather than the Zaire ebolavirus responsible for DRC’s 2018–2020 outbreak. WHO states that no approved vaccine or specific treatment existed for this virus as the 2026 outbreak began, although candidate countermeasures were being studied.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Transmission began in Ituri Province, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara and Bunia health zones, and later spread to other DRC provinces. Uganda’s cases were linked to transmission originating in DRC, making this a cross-border regional outbreak rather than an outbreak confined to one locality.

facts.label: International health status
facts.value: On May 17, 2026, the WHO Director-General determined that the epidemic in DRC and Uganda constituted a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations, while stating that it did not meet the separate criteria for a pandemic emergency.

facts.label: Response approach
facts.value: The response is led by the national health authorities with WHO and partner support, emphasizing rapid detection and laboratory confirmation, isolation and clinical care, contact tracing, infection prevention, safe burials, community engagement, and cross-border preparedness.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major reported developments in the 2026 DRC outbreak—such as reported tolls, geographic or regional status, treatment capacity, and workforce issues—rather than providing a complete case ledger, every official situation report, or the full history of Ebola in Central Africa.

explore_lenses.label: Who is most affected, and why is spread hard to stop?
explore_lenses.title: Ituri bears most of the burden
explore_lenses.summary: The outbreak is concentrated in northeastern DRC, especially Ituri, but transmission has expanded across multiple provinces. Conflict, displacement, population movement and missed community cases are limiting surveillance and timely care.

claims.text: As of 12 August, WHO said about 90% of confirmed cases and 80% of deaths were in Ituri, with sustained transmission in Bunia, Rwampara, Nizi and Lita.
WHO reported that the outbreak is unfolding amid insecurity, displacement, limited basic services and restricted access for response teams; these conditions raise the risk of undetected transmission.

Health workers are also affected: WHO recorded 119 confirmed infections and 36 deaths among health workers by 15 July, citing persistent occupational exposure and gaps in infection prevention and control.
WHO says community evidence points to practical barriers to care, including ambulance delays, limited treatment-centre reception capacity and uncertainty around laboratory-result communication.

explore_lenses.label: What does the evidence say about treatment and prevention?
explore_lenses.title: Care helps, but targeted tools remain unproven
explore_lenses.summary: This outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccine or specific treatment was available as of 17 August. Supportive clinical care, isolation, contact tracing and safe burials remain the established response measures while candidate products are tested.

claims.text: CDC states that no FDA-licensed or authorized vaccine protects against Bundibugyo virus; the U.S.-licensed ERVEBO vaccine targets Zaire ebolavirus and is not expected to protect against Bundibugyo virus.

WHO says outbreak control relies on rapid identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and community engagement because approved Bundibugyo-specific vaccines and treatments do not yet exist.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines had entered phase-one human safety trials, while the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS treatment trial had enrolled 100 patients.

WHO says it does not yet know whether the Zaire ebolavirus vaccine being considered for a phase-three trial is effective against Bundibugyo disease in humans, despite encouraging animal cross-protection findings.

story_report.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed the 2018–2020 epidemic as the country’s deadliest, with the public health institute reporting 4,945 confirmed cases and at least 2,325 deaths on 17 August. Reported deaths were occurring at a rate of one every 30 minutes. The toll has intensified pressure on response efforts in areas where transmission remains sustained and access to care and surveillance is constrained.

sections.heading: Transmission Concentrated in Ituri Province
sections.body: As of 12 August, the World Health Organization said about 90% of confirmed cases and 80% of deaths were in Ituri, with sustained transmission in Bunia, Rwampara, Nizi and Lita. The agency said insecurity, displacement, limited basic services and restricted access for response teams increase the risk that infections will go undetected. Health workers have also been heavily affected: by 15 July, WHO had recorded 119 confirmed infections and 36 deaths among them, citing occupational exposure and gaps in infection prevention and control.

sections.heading: Bundibugyo Response Relies on Core Measures
sections.body: WHO says control depends on rapidly identifying, isolating and caring for patients; tracing contacts; conducting safe burials; and engaging communities, because no approved Bundibugyo-specific vaccine or treatment exists. The U.S.-licensed ERVEBO vaccine targets Zaire ebolavirus and is not expected to protect against Bundibugyo virus, according to the CDC. Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines have entered phase-one safety trials, while the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS treatment trial has enrolled 100 patients.

unresolved.text: Case totals, geographic distribution and health-worker figures may change as delayed reports are verified, cases are reclassified and government situation reports are retrospectively revised; newly reported cases or deaths may reflect reporting backlogs rather than recent infections.

The effectiveness of candidate vaccines and treatments remains unknown. Early safety studies and the ongoing treatment trial cannot establish clinical effectiveness until results are available, and WHO does not know whether a Zaire ebolavirus vaccine under consideration for a phase-three trial protects people against Bundibugyo disease.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on 12 August that the epidemic was on track, at its then-current pace, to exceed the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak. That remains a projection; the eventual toll will depend on improvements in surveillance, care access, contact tracing, safe burials and security conditions.

related_stories.title: Indonesia Earthquake Causes Deaths and Displacement Amid Ongoing Aftershocks
related_stories.summary: A powerful earthquake struck Indonesia, resulting in at least 68 confirmed deaths and thousands displaced. The earthquake, which had magnitudes of 7.7 and 6.4, triggered nearly 1,600 aftershocks, complicating rescue efforts. Many survivors are awaiting aid as search and rescue operations continue in the affected areas, particularly on Flores island, where significant damage to homes and public buildings has been reported.

related_stories.title: Seven Dead in Stampede at Hindu Temple in Bihar, India
related_stories.summary: A stampede at a Hindu temple in Bihar, India, resulted in the deaths of seven people and injuries to at least nineteen others. The incident occurred amid a rush of devotees, reportedly triggered by panic over rumors of an electricity pole falling on worshippers. An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the stampede is currently underway.
